quickAnswer: Periodic restoration for commercial engineered and solid hardwood ranges from $0.35 to $0.75 per square foot for quarterly deep auto-scrubber cleaning and polymer conditioning, $1.25 to $2.50 per square foot for an annual screen-and-recoat (or chemical abrasion recoat), and $4.50 to $8.00+ per square foot for full dustless drum-sanding down to bare wood. Rolling periodic deep care into a monthly janitorial contract typically adds $0.03 to $0.06 per square foot per month.

blocks.text: The Three Tiers of Periodic Hardwood Restoration in Commercial Buildings

Unlike vinyl composition tile (VCT) that can be chemically stripped with high-pH amine strippers and recoated with acrylic wax four times a year, commercial engineered and solid hardwood depends on a permanent or semi-permanent protective wear layer—most commonly factory-applied UV-cured aluminum oxide urethane, site-applied two-component waterborne polyurethane, or penetrating hardwax oil. Once pedestrian traffic grinds through that protective film and exposes raw wood fibers to moisture and dirt, simple cleaning can no longer restore the appearance.

For US facility managers overseeing Class A corporate lobbies, executive suites, and multi-tenant corridors, periodic hardwood restoration falls into three distinct pricing and operational tiers based on how deeply the wear layer has degraded. Because specialty floor restoration technicians bill between $55 and $95 per labor hour (compared to $35 to $65 per hour for general nightly housekeeping), executing the right preventive tier at the right interval is the single highest-leverage decision in wood floor budgeting.

blocks.text: Tier 1: Quarterly Deep Extraction Scrubbing and Refresher Application ($0.35–$0.75/Sq Ft)

Even when nightly janitorial crews follow the 1.08x low-moisture microfiber protocol, microscopic grease, body oils, atmospheric soot, and polymer residues gradually settle into the wood grain texture and micro-bevels of commercial planks. Every 90 to 120 days, high-traffic hardwood zones benefit from a mechanized deep extraction scrub—often bundled into a building's Quarterly Deep Floor Care program at an amortized monthly cost of $0.03 to $0.06 per square foot.

During a Tier 1 service, specialty technicians use a dedicated cylindrical-brush hardwood auto-scrubber that dispenses a low-foaming wood cleaner, agitates out embedded soil from open oak grain and micro-bevels, and immediately vacuum-extracts 98% of the solution with a tight urethane squeegee so zero moisture penetrates the seams. If the floor has minor micro-scratches, technicians can follow with a compatible waterborne polyurethane maintenance refresher coat that fills superficial scuffs without requiring mechanical sanding.

blocks.title: Never Permit Acrylic VCT Wax or Mop-and-Glow Restorers on Hardwood
blocks.text: Unqualified janitorial subcontractors sometimes apply standard acrylic VCT floor finish over dull commercial hardwood to create a cheap instant shine. Acrylic wax does not bond permanently to polyurethane; it turns cloudy white when damp, peels in traffic lanes, and ruins the surface so that legitimate urethane recoats cannot adhere without costly chemical stripping.
Tier 2: Annual Screen-and-Recoat vs. Chemical Abrasion Systems ($1.25–$2.50/Sq Ft)

A screen-and-recoat (also called a buff-and-coat) is the workhorse preventive restoration procedure for commercial wood floors. Performed every 12 to 24 months depending on pedestrian volume, this process abrades only the top 10% to 15% of the existing clear polyurethane wear layer—never cutting down into the stained wood veneer—and applies one or two fresh coats of commercial two-component (2K) waterborne polyurethane.

On factory-finished engineered hardwood coated with aluminum oxide, traditional 120-grit or 150-grit mesh screening discs sometimes struggle to scratch the ultra-hard ceramic oxide surface evenly. In these buildings, certified commercial wood contractors often utilize a chemical bonding prep system alongside maroon conditioning pads to create a molecular covalent bond between the factory aluminum oxide coat and the new commercial waterborne urethane topcoat.

items.name: Step 1: Contaminant Testing and Wax Verification
items.text: Technicians test an inconspicuous corner for silicone furniture polish, acrylic VCT wax, or oil-soap residue. Any foreign contamination will cause the new $80-per-gallon waterborne urethane to craw, fish-eye, or peel within weeks.

items.name: Step 2: Dry HEPA Vacuuming and Deep Solvent/Surfactant Tack
items.text: The entire floor plate is vacuumed with HEPA filtration and tacked with an alcohol-based or manufacturer-certified prep cleaner to strip away surface lipids and shoe rubber.

items.name: Step 3: Low-Speed Mechanical Abrasion (175 RPM)
items.text: Using a 175 RPM rotary buffer or orbital multi-disc machine fitted with a 150-grit to 180-grit conditioning screen or maroon prep pad and dust-containment skirt, technicians create a uniform microscopic tooth across the old urethane.

items.name: Step 4: Commercial 2K Waterborne Polyurethane Application
items.text: Technicians apply a catalyzed two-component commercial waterborne urethane at a coverage rate of 500 to 600 sq ft per gallon using a weighted T-bar or microfiber roller, maintaining a wet edge across the wood grain.

blocks.text: Tier 3: Full Drum Sanding & Veneer Thickness Constraints ($4.50–$8.00/Sq Ft)

When a facility defers Tier 2 recoating for five or more years, foot traffic inevitably wears completely through the clear urethane coat in elevator lobbies, reception pivots, and coffee bar queues. Once raw wood turns gray or black from oxidized moisture and foot oils, a screen-and-recoat can no longer save the floor. The only remedy is Tier 3: sanding the entire floor down to bare wood with heavy drum or belt sanders, edge sanders, and planetary buffer systems, followed by stain and three coats of commercial sealer and finish.

Before approving a $4.50 to $8.00 per square foot sanding bid on engineered hardwood, facility directors must verify the thickness of the top hardwood wear layer (lamella). While traditional 3/4-inch solid oak hardwood can be sanded and refinished 5 to 7 times over a 50-year building lifecycle, commercial engineered hardwood varies wildly:

items: 0.6 mm to 1.5 mm Rotary-Peeled or Sliced Veneer: Cannot be drum-sanded even once without cutting directly into the plywood or HDF core. Only eligible for Tier 1 deep scrubbing and Tier 2 chemical screen-and-recoat.
2.0 mm to 2.5 mm Engineered Wear Layer: Can typically withstand 1 light professional sanding over its lifetime if the subfloor is dead-flat and free of high spots.
3.0 mm to 4.0 mm+ Commercial Architectural Wear Layer: Can be sanded and fully refinished 2 to 3 times over a 20- to 30-year lease lifecycle, comparable to solid wood above the tongue.
Over-Wood & Bevel Loss Consideration: Full sanding removes micro-beveled edges and flattens wire-brushed or hand-scraped textures, permanently altering the floor's original architectural aesthetic.

blocks.text: Coordinating Touchpoint Disinfection and Perimeter Detailing Around Restoration

During quarterly or annual hardwood restoration shutdowns, facility managers frequently bundle adjacent detail work—such as glass partition cleaning, restroom tile brightening, and high-touch disinfection—while furniture is moved out of the zones. However, chemical isolation around freshly abraded or recoated hardwood is critical so harsh sprays do not drift onto curing urethane.

For high-touch office surfaces, door hardware, and breakroom counters adjacent to hardwood zones, crews often deploy CloroxPro Hydrogen Peroxide Cleaner Disinfectant Concentrate, which achieves a 30-second to 1-minute hospital-grade disinfection contact time without harsh VOC fumes or bleach residues that could bleach wood stains. For ceramic tile restrooms and grout borders abutting hardwood corridors, Spartan Clean by Peroxy All-Purpose Cleaner Gallon (4-Case) provides Green Seal GS-37 certified hydrogen-peroxide surfactant cleaning to lift grout soil safely. Meanwhile, when cleaning floor-to-ceiling conference room glass and lobby curtain walls above hardwood floors, technicians using Zep Commercial Streak-Free Glass Cleaner Gallon (4-Case) should spray the ammonia-based formula directly onto a microfiber cloth rather than misting the glass directly, preventing ammonia overspray from dulling or spotting fresh waterborne wood finishes below.

blocks.title: LEED & Indoor Air Quality (IAQ) Compliance During Recoating
blocks.text: In multi-tenant Class A office towers, oil-modified polyurethanes and acid-cured conversion varnishes with VOC levels exceeding 350–550 g/L are typically prohibited by building management rules. Always specify low-VOC (<100–150 g/L) Greenguard Gold certified two-component waterborne commercial polyurethanes so adjacent tenant floors do not experience solvent odor migration through HVAC plenums.

faqs.q: Should we pay for hardwood screen-and-recoat services as a lump sum or amortize them into our monthly janitorial contract?
faqs.a: Amortizing periodic floor care into your monthly agreement (typically $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month for quarterly deep care, or $0.05 to $0.10 per sq ft per month including an annual recoat) protects the floor from budget cuts, provided your contract explicitly specifies the exact calendar months, square footage, and two-component urethane product to be applied. Without written milestone triggers, unscrupulous vendors may pocket the monthly amortization without executing the annual recoat.

faqs.q: How long must an office corridor remain closed to foot traffic after a commercial screen-and-recoat?
faqs.a: With modern commercial two-component waterborne polyurethanes, the finish is typically dry to the touch in 2 to 3 hours, ready for light stocking-foot or clean sneaker traffic in 12 to 24 hours, and ready for furniture replacement after 24 to 48 hours. Full chemical cross-linking takes 5 to 7 days, during which wet mopping and area rug placement must be suspended.

faqs.q: Why did our contractor quote $6.50 per square foot to refinish our hardwood lobby when another bid was $1.80 per square foot?
faqs.a: Those two bids are pricing completely different scopes. The $1.80/sq ft bid is a Tier 2 screen-and-recoat (light surface abrasion plus 1 coat of urethane completed in a single night), whereas the $6.50/sq ft bid is a Tier 3 full multi-grit drum sanding down to bare wood plus stain and 3 coats of commercial urethane over a 3-day weekend shutdown.

faqs.q: What insurance endorsements should we verify before allowing a contractor to sand or recoat commercial hardwood?
faqs.a: Verify a minimum $2,000,000 General Liability COI with Completed Operations coverage and confirm the contractor carries inland marine / property-in-care coverage. If a crew sands through a 1.5 mm engineered veneer or applies a contaminated finish that peels across 5,000 sq ft, replacing the ruined architectural wood floor can easily exceed $60,000 to $100,000.
